name: Reuben Louis Rosenberg
summary: South African-born mathematician and numerical analyst known for the Stein–Rosenberg theorem on iterative methods for linear equations.

name: Philip Bernard Stein
summary: South African mathematician and collaborator of Rosenberg on the Stein–Rosenberg theorem.

name: Violet Eva Hatcher
summary: Wife of Reuben Louis Rosenberg, married in 1937.

name: University of Cape Town
summary: University in Cape Town, South Africa, where Rosenberg completed his BA and MA.

name: University of the Witwatersrand
summary: University in Johannesburg where Rosenberg worked as a Junior Lecturer in 1930.

name: Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität zu Berlin
summary: University in Berlin where Rosenberg earned his doctorate in nuclear physics.

name: Imperial College of Science, Technology, and Medicine
summary: London institution where Rosenberg held a Beit Fellowship and obtained a D.I.C.

name: Natal University College
summary: College in Pietermaritzburg where Rosenberg worked from 1935 to 1949.

name: Bristol University
summary: University where Rosenberg conducted research in Atomic Physics on leave in 1947–1948.

name: Chelsea Polytechnic
aliases: Chelsea College of Science and Technology
summary: London institution where Rosenberg was a Senior Lecturer from 1949 to 1955.

name: University of New Brunswick
summary: Canadian university where Rosenberg was a professor from 1955 to 1966.

name: National Research Council
summary: Canadian research organization where Rosenberg was affiliated from 1960 to 1963.

name: Carleton University
summary: Ottawa university where Rosenberg worked from 1966 until retirement and beyond.

name: Johannesburg
summary: City in South Africa where Rosenberg was born.

name: London
summary: City in England where Rosenberg married and worked at Imperial College and Chelsea Polytechnic.

name: Ottawa
summary: City in Canada where Rosenberg died and worked at Carleton University.

name: On the solution of linear simultaneous equations by iteration
summary: 1948 paper by Stein and Rosenberg establishing the Stein–Rosenberg theorem on iterative methods.
